content: Uterine contractions can be monitored using either external tocodynamometry (ET) or internal tocodynamometry (IT), the latter of which is only possible after the rupture of membranes. Monitoring the frequency of uterine contractions is particularly important when intravenous oxytocin is administered, as excessive uterine activity, such as hyperstimulation or tachysystole, can lead to fetal distress. Some clinicians prefer IT over ET during labour induction or augmentation with oxytocin because intrauterine pressure catheters provide more accurate measurements of uterine activity compared to external devices. However, IT is associated with higher costs and potential risks to both the mother and the fetus. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of IT compared to ET in cases where intravenous oxytocin was used for labour induction or augmentation. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (up to March 31, 2013) and PubMed (from 1966 to April 6, 2013). Only published randomised controlled trials comparing IT and ET in women undergoing induced or augmented labour with oxytocin were included. Trials using quasi-randomised methods of treatment allocation were excluded. No unpublished or ongoing studies on this topic were identified. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of the trials, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The accuracy of the data was verified, and study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. Three studies involving a total of 1,945 women met the inclusion criteria. The overall risk of bias across the three trials was mixed. No serious complications were reported in any of the trials, and there were no maternal or neonatal deaths. Neonatal outcomes did not differ significantly between the IT and ET groups. Specifically, the risk of an Apgar score below seven at five minutes was not statistically different (RR 1.78, 95% CI 0.83 to 3.83; three studies, n = 1,945). Similarly, there was no significant difference in the risk of umbilical artery pH below 7.15 (RR 1.31, 95% CI 0.95 to 1.79; one study, n = 1,456) or below 7.16 (RR 1.23, 95% CI 0.39 to 3.92; one study, n = 239). Admission to the neonatal intensive care unit (RR 0.34, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.67; two studies, n = 489) and hospitalisation for more than 48 hours (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.71 to 1.20; one study, n = 1,456) were also not significantly different between the groups. The pooled risk of instrumental delivery, including caesarean section, ventouse, and forceps extraction, was not statistically significantly different between the IT and ET groups (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.21; three studies, n = 1,945). Hyperstimulation was reported in two studies (n = 489), but there was no statistically significant difference between the groups (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.88). In conclusion, this review found no significant differences in maternal or neonatal outcomes between internal and external tocodynamometry when intravenous oxytocin was used for labour induction or augmentation. However, given that the review is based on three studies of moderate quality involving 1,945 women, the evidence is insufficient to recommend one method of tocodynamometry over the other in this clinical context.
